definition.text: Present value is what a stream of expected future payments is worth as of today.

facts.text: Present value is usually below future value because money held now can earn interest, which is called the time value of money.
Put simply, a dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow, since today's dollar can be invested and earn a day's interest.
If a zero-coupon $100 note payable in one year sells for $80 now, $80 is its present value.
Working out what money today will be worth later is called capitalization; the reverse, valuing future money today, is discounting.
The usual model uses compound interest, and (1 + i) to the power −n is called the present value factor.
The net present value of a stream of cash flows discounts each flow to the present and adds them up.
A risk-free interest rate is used for riskless projects; for risky ones a risk premium is added, judged from projects with similar risks.
When both timing and size of cash flows are uncertain, an expected present value approach weighs several scenarios by their probabilities.

title: Perpetuity
article: Present value#Present value of a perpetuity

definition.text: A perpetuity is a series of regular payments that continues indefinitely.

facts.text: Few such instruments actually exist.
Its present value is the limit of the annuity formula as the number of payments goes to infinity.
A perpetuity immediate pays at the end of each period and a perpetuity due at the start; their values differ by a factor of (1 + i).

definition.text: Years' purchase is the traditional way of valuing an income stream by multiplying its average expected yearly cash flow by a fixed number.

facts.text: A lease paying $10,000 a year sold at 20 years' purchase is valued at $200,000, which equals discounting in perpetuity at 5%.
Buyers of riskier income pay fewer years' purchase.
The English crown used it to set resale prices for manors seized at the Dissolution of the Monasteries in the early 16th century.

definition.text: Risk aversion is the tendency to prefer a more certain outcome to a riskier one, even when the risky option pays the same or more on average.

facts.text: A risk-averse investor may choose a bank account with a low guaranteed rate over shares that could pay more but might lose value.
Offered a sure $50 or a coin flip for $100 or nothing, a risk-averse person would accept a sure amount below $50, such as $40.
A risk-neutral person is indifferent between the bet and a sure $50; a risk-loving person takes the bet even against a sure $60.
The certainty equivalent is the smallest sure amount a person would accept instead of a gamble; it is a measure of risk aversion.
The risk premium is the gap between a gamble's expected value and its certainty equivalent, positive for the risk-averse.
In expected utility theory a person is risk-averse exactly when their utility function is concave.
On average, higher earners are less risk-averse than lower earners.

title: Arrow–Pratt measures of risk aversion

definition.text: The Arrow–Pratt measures express how risk-averse a person is from the curvature of their utility function, in absolute or relative terms.

facts.text: The more curved the utility function, the higher the risk aversion.
Absolute risk aversion is named after economists Kenneth Arrow and John W. Pratt and is built from the first and second derivatives of utility.
Relative risk aversion has no units, so it can be compared across settings; logarithmic utility gives a constant relative risk aversion of 1.
In intertemporal choice problems, relative risk aversion often cannot be separated from the elasticity of intertemporal substitution.

distinct_from: Rabin's critique of expected utility risk aversion

title: Rabin's critique of expected utility risk aversion
article: Risk aversion#Limitations of expected utility treatment of risk aversion

definition.text: Rabin's calibration theorem criticises using expected utility theory to explain risk aversion in small-stakes decisions.

facts.text: It shows that someone who always refuses a 50–50 bet to lose $100 or gain $110 would also refuse a 50–50 bet to lose $1,000 or gain any sum.
Rabin finds this implausible: small-stakes aversion from diminishing marginal utility would imply extreme aversion at large stakes.
Prospect theory answers this by judging outcomes against a reference point, usually the status quo, rather than final wealth.

contested_note: Rabin argues the expected utility account of small-stakes risk aversion is implausible; prospect theory offers an alternative.

title: Risk aversion in public policy
article: Risk aversion#Public understanding and risk in social activities

definition.text: Many government agencies have risk-averse mandates that require risks to be minimised, sometimes at the cost of the benefits of the risky activity.

facts.text: Reducing a risk has an opportunity cost: the value lost by not taking the risky action.
Laws focused on risk without weighing its benefits may misrepresent society's goals.
Risk-averse planning of schools and playgrounds often keeps children from activities they would otherwise benefit from.

distinct_from: Rabin's critique of expected utility risk aversion
